set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: Which recording shows the atonia of voluntary muscles during rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Correct. The electromyogram, the muscle recording, shows atonia of voluntary muscles in rapid eye movement sleep, sparing the eye muscles and diaphragm, as inactivity due to inhibited alpha motor neurons.

The electrooculogram records the eyes, and in rapid eye movement sleep it shows irregular, sharply peaked eye movements, not voluntary muscle atonia. Tell: the eye recording shows eye movements; the muscle recording shows atonia.

The electroencephalogram records brain waves: in rapid eye movement sleep a mixed, low-voltage pattern with sawtooth waves and beta waves like wakefulness. It does not measure muscle tone. Tell: brain waves are not muscle tone.

Blood pressure tracks vascular changes, falling by 10 to 30% in non-rapid eye movement sleep along with decreased peripheral vascular tone; it does not show voluntary muscle activity. Tell: atonia is read from the muscle recording.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 12, 28

set1.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set1.q: Which wave is seen in infancy and in very deep sleep?
opts: Theta waves appear over the parietal and temporal regions in children and during emotional stress in some adults, but very deep sleep is marked by delta, not theta. Tell: very deep sleep settles the choice in favor of delta.

Alpha waves, 8 to 13 cycles per second, mark quiet, resting wakefulness in almost all healthy adults and disappear during deep sleep, so they cannot be the wave of very deep sleep. Tell: alpha vanishes exactly where delta appears.
Beta waves are fast and low in voltage, belonging to alert wakefulness and rapid eye movement sleep, not to infancy or very deep sleep. Tell: deep sleep and infancy share the slow, high-voltage wave.

Correct. Delta waves, below 3.5 cycles per second with voltages 2 to 4 times greater than most other waves, occur in very deep sleep, in infancy, and in persons with serious organic brain disease. Deep sleep marked by delta is stage N3.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 25, 26

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: During sleep, the electroencephalogram shows high-voltage waves slower than 3.5 cycles per second. Which stage fits?
opts: Correct. Waves slower than 3.5 cycles per second with high voltage are delta waves, and delta waves mark stage N3, the deep, restful and deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, in which body and tissue growth and repair occur.
Stage N1 is the light, drowsy transition from wakefulness, when the electroencephalogram voltage becomes low, not high. Tell: high-voltage waves below 3.5 cycles per second mean the deepest stage.
Stage N2 shows theta waves, 4 to 7 cycles per second, faster than the waves described and without delta's high voltage. Tell: below 3.5 cycles per second is delta, and delta marks N3.
Rapid eye movement sleep shows a mixed, low-voltage pattern with beta waves like wakefulness, the opposite of slow, high-voltage waves. Tell: fast and low in voltage is rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 25, 26, 27, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set1.q: In an unconscious person, which observation points to coma rather than sleep?
opts: Delta waves, below 3.5 cycles per second, occur in very deep sleep, so slow waves alone do not distinguish coma from sleep. Tell: the deciding observation is whether a stimulus arouses the person, not the wave frequency.

Correct. Arousability separates the two states: sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli, and coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused. Failure to rouse to any stimulus points to coma.

Very depressed muscle tone, with atonia of voluntary muscles, is expected in rapid eye movement sleep, so it does not set coma apart from sleep. Tell: atonia is a normal sleep finding; absent arousal is what defines coma.
Slow heart rate, low blood pressure

A slow heart rate and low blood pressure, from increased parasympathetic tone, are normal in non-rapid eye movement sleep, when these values fall by 10 to 30%. Tell: these vital-sign changes occur in ordinary sleep, so they cannot mark coma.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 10, 12, 14, 26, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set1.q: Where are the reticular activating nuclei that start wakefulness located?
opts: The thalamus appears in the delta-wave findings: when the cerebral cortex is separated from the thalamus in animals, delta waves persist in the cortex. The activating nuclei named in the model are mesencephalic and upper pontine. Tell: thalamic separation is a delta-wave fact.

The parietal and frontal regions are where beta waves are recorded during specific activation of those areas; that cortex is a target of the activating nuclei, not their site. Tell: the nuclei lie below the cortex, in the mesencephalon and upper pons.

Correct. The proposed model names the mesencephalic and upper pontine reticular activating nuclei. Released from inhibition, they activate spontaneously, excite the cerebral cortex and peripheral nervous system, and receive positive feedback from the cortex.

The occipital region is where alpha waves are recorded most intensely in a quiet, resting adult; it is part of the cortex that the activating nuclei excite, not where the nuclei lie. Tell: the activating nuclei sit in the mesencephalon and upper pons.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 18, 22, 23, 26

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: Which state combines vivid dreaming, irregular heart and breathing rates, and very depressed muscle tone?
opts: Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep is the active, dreaming form of sleep: dreams are vivid, heart and breathing rates become irregular, and muscle tone is very depressed, with atonia of voluntary muscles except the eyes and diaphragm.

Non-rapid eye movement sleep has less vivid dreams and increased parasympathetic tone with a slow heart rate and decreased breathing rate, so irregular vital signs and vivid dreaming do not fit. Tell: steady slowing and dimmer dreams mean non-rapid eye movement sleep.
Quiet wakefulness is a relaxed, awake state with the eyes closed and alpha waves; the person is not dreaming and has no sleep atonia. Tell: dreaming requires sleep, so no waking state fits.
ruled out by a stated finding

Alert wakefulness shares beta waves with rapid eye movement sleep, but the person is awake and processing information, not dreaming with very depressed muscle tone. Tell: beta waves plus atonia and dreams means rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 10, 14, 27, 28

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: Which function of sleep concerns development of the nervous system?
opts: Targeted erasure of synapses removes connections so the brain can forget unimportant information that might clutter the synaptic network; it prunes rather than develops. Tell: pruning is erasure; development is maturation.

Conservation of metabolic energy concerns the body's energy budget, not the development of nerve tissue. Tell: energy saving and neural development are separate functions of sleep, and only maturation describes development.

Clearance of metabolic waste removes products generated by neural activity in the awake brain; it cleans up after activity rather than developing the nervous system. Tell: cleanup is clearance; growth of the nervous system is maturation.

Correct. Neural maturation is one of the functions of sleep and concerns the developing nervous system. The other functions named are facilitation of learning or memory, targeted synapse erasure, cognition, clearance of metabolic waste and conservation of metabolic energy.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: What causes the muscle inactivity of rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Correct. The atonia of rapid eye movement sleep is inactivity due to inhibited alpha motor neurons, which matches the very depressed muscle tone that indicates inhibition of the spinal muscle control areas. The eye muscles and diaphragm are spared.

Fatigue of reticular activating neurons, after many hours awake, explains the transition from wakefulness to sleep, not muscle atonia within rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: atonia comes from inhibition of motor neurons, not from fatigue of the activating system.

Increased parasympathetic tone is a physiologic change of non-rapid eye movement sleep, with low blood pressure and a slow heart rate. It does not explain the atonia of rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: parasympathetic tone is a non-rapid eye movement change.

Decreased peripheral vascular tone accompanies non-rapid eye movement sleep along with falling blood pressure and heart rate; it concerns blood vessels, not voluntary muscle activity. Tell: vascular tone is not skeletal muscle tone.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 14, 19, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: What shared electroencephalogram pattern makes rapid eye movement sleep hard to tell from alert wakefulness?
opts: Waves of 4 to 7 cycles per second

Waves of 4 to 7 cycles per second are theta waves, listed for stage N2 and seen in children and during emotional stress. They are slower than the pattern of alert wakefulness. Tell: the shared pattern is high in frequency.

Correct. In rapid eye movement sleep the waves are irregular and high in frequency, beta waves like those of an awake, active person, which makes it often difficult to tell rapid eye movement sleep from alert wakefulness. Atonia of voluntary muscles is the difference.

Rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second are alpha waves of quiet, resting wakefulness, not the pattern shared by rapid eye movement sleep and alert wakefulness. Tell: the shared pattern is irregular and fast.

High-voltage, low-frequency waves are the delta waves of stage N3 and infancy; neither rapid eye movement sleep nor alert wakefulness shows them. Tell: deep sleep is slow and large; the alert pattern is fast and small.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 25, 26, 28, 29

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: After someone stays awake for more than 24 hours, what is sleep like in the first hour after falling asleep?
opts: Rapid eye movement with vivid dreams

When a person is extremely sleepy, rapid eye movement episodes are short or even absent, so vivid-dream sleep does not fill that first hour. Tell: sleepiness shortens rapid eye movement sleep, and early sleep after a long time awake is deep.

Light, drowsy sleep describes stage N1, the transition from wakefulness. After a long period awake, the first hour is described as deep sleep, not light. Tell: a long time awake brings deep sleep early.

Irregular heart and breathing rates mark rapid eye movement sleep, the dream state, which is not restful. The deep sleep after long wakefulness is extremely restful, with a decreased breathing rate. Tell: restful and steadily slowed is non-rapid eye movement sleep.

Correct. After more than 24 hours awake, the sleep in the first hour after going to sleep is deep, extremely restful non-rapid eye movement sleep, with blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate and metabolic rate falling by 10 to 30%.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 10, 12, 28

set1.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set1.q: Which wave runs below 3.5 cycles per second, has voltages 2 to 4 times greater than most other waves, and appears in serious organic brain disease?
opts: Alpha waves run at 8 to 13 cycles per second, the rhythm of a healthy, awake adult at rest, and they disappear during deep sleep. Tell: a frequency below 3.5 excludes alpha.
ruled out by a stated finding
Beta waves are fast, above 14 cycles per second, and low in voltage, the reverse of the slow, high-voltage pattern described. Tell: low voltage is beta, high voltage is delta.

Theta waves also appear in many brain disorders, especially degenerative brain states, but they run at 4 to 7 cycles per second without the large voltage of delta. Tell: below 3.5 with 2 to 4 times the voltage is delta.

Correct. Delta waves include all waves below 3.5 cycles per second, often with voltages 2 to 4 times greater than other brain waves, and they occur in very deep sleep, in infancy and in persons with serious organic brain disease.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 25, 26

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: During which stage does body and tissue growth and repair occur?
opts: Stage N2 is deeper and less responsive than N1, with falling heart rate and temperature, and it is the longest stage by total duration, but body and tissue repair is tied to N3. Tell: the longest stage is N2; the repair stage is N3.

Rapid eye movement sleep is active, dreaming sleep with brain waves like wakefulness and atonia of voluntary muscles, and it is not restful or deep. Tell: tissue growth and repair come with the deepest, restful stage, N3.

Correct. Stage N3, the deep, restful and deepest non-rapid eye movement stage marked by delta waves, is when body and tissue growth and repair occur. It is concentrated in the early cycles of the night and is also the stage that decreases with age.

Stage N1 is the drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep. Growth and repair are tied to the deepest stage of non-rapid eye movement sleep, not to this light one. Tell: light, transitional sleep is N1; repair belongs to N3.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 10, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: Across a typical night, when is the deepest non-rapid eye movement sleep concentrated?
opts: By the middle of the night the cycles no longer reach the depth seen at the start, and the rapid eye movement periods are growing longer. Tell: depth peaks early, not midway through the night.

The final cycles are the lightest and end with rapid eye movement sleep, from which people can awaken spontaneously in the morning. Tell: late night favors rapid eye movement sleep; early night holds the deepest sleep.

The cycles are not identical: the early ones reach the deepest stages and the later ones are shallower, with longer rapid eye movement periods. Tell: deep sleep is front-loaded into the first cycles of the night.

Correct. A plot of sleep stages across a night shows the deepest non-rapid eye movement stages in the first cycles, while later cycles stay lighter and their rapid eye movement periods lengthen. Deep, extremely restful sleep is also described in the first hour after going to sleep.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 7, 10, 12

set1.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set1.q: Once wakefulness begins, what lets it sustain itself?
opts: Wakefulness begins when the sleep centers are not activated, which releases the activating nuclei from inhibition. Active sleep-promoting centers belong to the transition into sleep. Tell: the sleep centers are quiet while a person is awake.

Fatigue of activating-system neurons, after many hours of activity, makes the positive feedback cycle fade and lets sleep-promoting centers take over. Tell: fatigue ends wakefulness rather than sustaining it.

Correct. Once wakefulness begins it can sustain itself naturally: the excited cerebral cortex sends positive feedback signals back to the mesencephalic reticular activating nuclei, which keeps them active until their neurons fatigue after many hours.

The cortex sends positive, not negative, feedback to the reticular activating nuclei, so each keeps the other active. Negative feedback would damp wakefulness rather than sustain it. Tell: wakefulness is self-sustaining through positive feedback.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 18, 19

set1.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set1.q: When an awake, resting person directs attention to a specific mental task, what happens to the brain waves?
opts: Alpha waves give way to beta waves

Correct. When an awake person's attention is directed to a specific type of mental activity, alpha waves stop and are replaced by beta waves, the asynchronous, low-voltage waves of an alert brain actively processing information.
Beta waves give way to alpha waves

That is the reverse: alpha waves belong to quiet rest, and turning attention to a task replaces them with beta. Beta giving way to alpha fits relaxing with the eyes closed. Tell: concentration brings beta.
Alpha waves give way to theta waves
Theta waves appear during emotional stress in some adults, in children and in brain disorders, not with ordinary focused attention. Tell: mental effort produces beta, not theta.
Alpha waves give way to delta waves
Delta waves belong to very deep sleep, infancy and serious organic brain disease; they do not appear when an awake person concentrates. Tell: an awake, focused brain shows beta.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: During non-rapid eye movement sleep, by about how much do blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate and metabolic rate fall?
opts: A fall of 1 to 5% understates the change; the decrease in blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate and metabolic rate is 10 to 30%. Tell: the fall is tens of percent, not a few.

Correct. Non-rapid eye movement sleep is associated with decreased peripheral vascular tone and other vegetative bodily functions, with blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate and metabolic rate falling by 10 to 30%.

A fall of 40 to 60% overstates it; the decrease is 10 to 30%. For scale, the rise in brain metabolism during rapid eye movement sleep is up to 20%. Tell: the non-rapid eye movement changes stay within 10 to 30%.
A fall of 70 to 90% is far beyond the 10 to 30% decrease of normal non-rapid eye movement sleep, which is deep and restful rather than a collapse of bodily function. Tell: 10 to 30%.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 10, 12

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: Which function of sleep reduces the body's use of fuel?
opts: Clearance of metabolic waste removes products generated by neural activity in the awake brain; it disposes of waste rather than saving fuel. Tell: the same word metabolic appears in both, but clearance removes and conservation saves.
Neural maturation concerns development of the nervous system, not how much fuel the body uses. Tell: maturation is development; conservation of metabolic energy is the saving function.

Targeted erasure of synapses lets the brain forget unimportant information that might clutter the synaptic network; it manages stored information, not fuel use. Tell: erasure concerns clutter in the synaptic network.

Correct. Conservation of metabolic energy is one of the functions of sleep, and in non-rapid eye movement sleep the metabolic rate falls by 10 to 30%. It sits beside neural maturation, learning, targeted synapse erasure, cognition and clearance of metabolic waste.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 12, 17

set1.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set1.q: Which circumstance can bring out theta waves in an awake adult?
opts: Correct. Theta waves, 4 to 7 cycles per second, occur during emotional stress in some adults, especially during disappointment and frustration. They also appear in children's parietal and temporal regions and in many brain disorders, especially degenerative brain states.
Quiet, eyes-closed rest in an awake adult brings alpha waves, 8 to 13 cycles per second, strongest over the occipital region. Tell: relaxation means alpha; emotional stress can mean theta.
Directing attention to a specific mental task makes alpha waves stop and be replaced by beta waves, faster than 14 cycles per second. Tell: concentration brings beta, not theta.
Very deep sleep produces delta waves, below 3.5 cycles per second, and the stem describes an awake adult in any case. Tell: an awake adult with theta waves points to emotional stress.
ruled out by a stated finding
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 24, 25, 26, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: About how often does a rapid eye movement episode recur during sleep?
opts: Twenty minutes falls within the 5 to 30 minutes that a single episode lasts, not the gap between episodes. Episodes recur about every 90 minutes. Tell: episode length is a matter of minutes; recurrence tracks the 90-minute cycle.

Recurrence every 45 minutes would mean about ten episodes in 8 hours, double the 4 to 5 cycles of 90 to 120 minutes in an average night. Tell: there is one rapid eye movement episode per cycle, about every 90 minutes.

An hourly rhythm is shorter than a sleep cycle, which lasts 90 to 120 minutes. Rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes, once per cycle. Tell: match the recurrence to the length of the cycle.

Correct. Each rapid eye movement episode recurs about every 90 minutes, which matches sleep cycles of 90 to 120 minutes, 4 to 5 cycles in an average 8 hours of sleep. Each episode itself lasts 5 to 30 minutes.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 9

set1.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set1.q: States such as sleep, wakefulness and extreme excitement arise mainly from what?
opts: Blood pressure falls by 10 to 30% during non-rapid eye movement sleep, a consequence of the sleep state rather than its source. The states arise from activating or inhibiting forces within the brain. Tell: vital-sign changes follow a brain state; they do not generate it.

In the proposed sleep-wakefulness model, the reticular activating nuclei excite the cerebral cortex and the peripheral nervous system, so peripheral nerves sit downstream of the brain's activating forces. Tell: the drive starts within the brain and spreads outward.

Correct. Sleep, wakefulness, extreme excitement and different levels of mood are all states of brain activity, and for the most part each arises from activating or inhibiting forces generated within the brain itself, not from outside events.

Sensory and other stimuli can arouse a sleeping person, but the states themselves arise, for the most part, from activating or inhibiting forces generated within the brain. Tell: a stimulus can end sleep; it is not what creates each brain state.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 3, 5, 12, 18

set1.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set1.q: What happens in the deepest stage of non-rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: The drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep is stage N1, the lightest non-rapid eye movement stage, at the opposite end from the deepest stage. Tell: drowsy and light means N1; deepest means N3.

Irregular heart and breathing rates are characteristic of rapid eye movement sleep, the dream state. Non-rapid eye movement sleep brings a slow heart rate and a decreased breathing rate. Tell: irregular vital signs point to rapid eye movement sleep.
Body and tissue growth and repair

Correct. The deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, stage N3, is restful sleep marked by delta waves, and it is when body and tissue growth and repair occur. Its delta waves run below 3.5 cycles per second with high voltage, and the stage decreases with age.
Vivid dreaming with an active brain

Vivid dreaming with a very active brain marks rapid eye movement sleep, when overall brain metabolism can rise by as much as 20%. Non-rapid eye movement sleep brings less vivid dreams. Tell: active, vivid dreaming is rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 10, 14, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: How do heart rate and breathing rate behave during rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Correct. In rapid eye movement sleep heart rate and breathing rate become irregular, which is characteristic of the dream state, alongside rapid eye movements and an active brain. Non-rapid eye movement sleep instead brings a slow heart rate and a decreased breathing rate.

A 10 to 30% fall in heart rate, breathing rate, blood pressure and metabolic rate describes non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: a steady fall is non-rapid eye movement sleep; irregularity is rapid eye movement sleep.

Increased parasympathetic tone with a slow heart rate and decreased breathing rate is the physiology of non-rapid eye movement sleep, not of the dream state. Tell: parasympathetic slowing marks non-rapid eye movement sleep.

Overall brain metabolism can rise by up to 20% in rapid eye movement sleep, but heart and breathing rates do not climb steadily; they become irregular. Tell: the rhythm turns irregular rather than steadily faster.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 14

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: Why is rapid eye movement sleep also called desynchronized sleep?
opts: Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep is called desynchronized sleep because there is a lack of synchrony in neuron firing during its brain activity, which gives irregular, high-frequency waves on the electroencephalogram.
Dreams are not stored in memory
Lack of consolidation in memory explains why non-rapid eye movement dreams are often not remembered; it has nothing to do with the name desynchronized. Tell: the name describes neuron firing.
Waves are slow and high in voltage
Slow, high-voltage waves are the delta waves of stage N3; rapid eye movement sleep shows irregular, high-frequency waves. Tell: desynchronized activity is fast and irregular, not slow and large.
Heart and breathing rates are regular
Heart and breathing rates become irregular, not regular, during rapid eye movement sleep, and the name refers to neuron firing in any case. Tell: desynchronized means neurons firing out of step.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 13, 26, 29

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: About what share of a young adult's sleep time does rapid eye movement sleep occupy?
opts: About 10% understates it: rapid eye movement sleep fills about a quarter of a young adult's sleep, recurring about every 90 minutes through the night. Tell: one quarter, not one tenth.

Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep occurs in episodes and occupies about 25% of a young adult's sleep time, with an episode recurring about every 90 minutes and lasting 5 to 30 minutes. The majority of the sleep cycle is stage N2, a non-rapid eye movement stage.

Half the night would make rapid eye movement sleep the main sleep type, but the majority of the sleep cycle is stage N2, a non-rapid eye movement stage. Tell: rapid eye movement sleep is about a quarter; N2 is the majority.

Three quarters would leave little room for non-rapid eye movement sleep, yet stage N2 alone is the longest stage by total duration. Tell: rapid eye movement sleep takes about a quarter of a young adult's sleep time.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 13, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: Which stage is the drowsy transition from wakefulness into light sleep?
opts: Stage N3 is the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, deep restful sleep with delta waves, far from the drowsy edge of wakefulness. Tell: deepest is N3; lightest and transitional is N1.

Rapid eye movement sleep is the active dream state with atonia and awake-like brain waves, and in a typical night it follows the non-rapid eye movement stages rather than opening sleep. Tell: the doorway into sleep is N1.

Correct. Stage N1 is the transition from wakefulness: the person is somnolent or drowsy and in light sleep. It is the first, lightest non-rapid eye movement stage, and the electroencephalogram voltage becomes low.

Stage N2 follows N1 and is less responsive, deeper sleep, with falling heart rate and temperature; it is the longest stage by total duration. Tell: the drowsy transition is N1; deeper and longest is N2.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 7, 27, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: Which wave does the electroencephalogram show in stage N2?
opts: Delta waves, below 3.5 cycles per second and high in voltage, mark stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage. Stage N2 has not slowed that far. Tell: N3 is delta; N2 is theta.
Sawtooth waves are part of the mixed, low-voltage pattern of rapid eye movement sleep, not of a non-rapid eye movement stage. Tell: sawtooth waves mean rapid eye movement sleep.

Correct. Stage N2, the less responsive, deeper sleep that is the longest stage by total duration, shows theta waves, 4 to 7 cycles per second, on the electroencephalogram. Delta waves wait for stage N3.

Beta waves mark the awake, eyes-open state and rapid eye movement sleep, whose waves resemble wakefulness. Stage N2 is slower. Tell: as non-rapid eye movement sleep deepens, the frequency slows away from beta.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 25, 28

set1.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.q: Which combination fits non-rapid eye movement sleep rather than rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Brain waves resembling wakefulness are the reason rapid eye movement sleep is called paradoxical sleep. Non-rapid eye movement sleep slows toward theta and delta waves. Tell: awake-like waves during sleep mean rapid eye movement sleep.
Low blood pressure, slow heart rate

Correct. Non-rapid eye movement sleep brings increased parasympathetic tone with low blood pressure, a slow heart rate and a decreased breathing rate, part of a 10 to 30% fall in vegetative functions. In rapid eye movement sleep, heart and breathing rates become irregular instead.

Irregular heart and breathing rates are characteristic of the dream state of rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: irregular vital signs point to rapid eye movement sleep; steady slowing points to non-rapid eye movement sleep.

Overall brain metabolism rises by up to 20% in rapid eye movement sleep because the brain is very active, whereas metabolic rate falls in non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: rising metabolism means rapid eye movement sleep.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 14, 28

set1.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set1.q: From which regions are beta waves recorded mainly?
opts: Temporal activity points to theta in children and occipital activity to resting alpha; neither region is the main source of beta. Tell: beta is recorded where the brain is being actively used, over the parietal and frontal regions.

Correct. Beta waves are recorded mainly from the parietal and frontal regions during specific activation of these parts of the brain, when a person is awake, alert and actively processing information.
The parietal and temporal regions are where theta waves, 4 to 7 cycles per second, appear in children. Tell: parietal with temporal points to theta; parietal with frontal points to beta.

The occipital region is the strongest source of alpha waves in a resting, awake adult, not of beta. Tell: occipital points to alpha; beta comes from parietal and frontal areas while they are being activated.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 25

set1.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set1.q: In which state does a mixed, low-voltage electroencephalogram with sawtooth waves appear?
opts: Stage N2 shows theta waves and is the longest stage by total duration; sawtooth waves are not part of its pattern. Tell: sawtooth waves belong to rapid eye movement sleep.
Stage N3 shows delta waves, slow and 2 to 4 times higher in voltage than most other waves, the opposite of a mixed, low-voltage pattern. Tell: deep sleep is high in voltage.

Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep shows a mixed, low-voltage electroencephalogram with sawtooth waves and beta activity similar to wakefulness, alongside irregular, sharply peaked eye movements and atonia of voluntary muscles.

Stage N1 is low in voltage too, but sawtooth waves are a rapid eye movement marker, not a feature of the drowsy transition from wakefulness. Tell: low voltage alone is not enough; the sawtooth waves decide.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 26, 27, 28

set1.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set1.q: Which wave is asynchronous and low in voltage, can reach 80 cycles per second, and appears when a person is actively processing information?
opts: Theta waves run at 4 to 7 cycles per second, far below 80, and appear in children, under emotional stress and in brain disorders. Tell: active information processing in an alert adult means beta.

Correct. Beta waves occur at frequencies greater than 14 cycles per second and as high as 80, are asynchronous and low in voltage, and are recorded mainly from the parietal and frontal regions when the person is awake, alert and actively processing information.

Alpha waves are rhythmical, not asynchronous, at 8 to 13 cycles per second, and belong to quiet rest; they stop and give way to beta when attention turns to a task. Tell: rhythmical and resting is alpha.

Delta waves are the opposite: below 3.5 cycles per second with voltages 2 to 4 times greater than most other waves, in very deep sleep. Tell: low voltage and fast is beta; high voltage and slow is delta.
set1.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 24, 25, 26

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: What happens to muscle tone during rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Tone falls, not rises: rapid eye movement sleep brings atonia of voluntary muscles, inactivity due to inhibited alpha motor neurons. Tell: the brain is active, but the body is atonic.

The brain waves of rapid eye movement sleep resemble the awake state, but the muscles do not: the beta waves come paired with atonia of voluntary muscles. Tell: an awake-looking brain sits in an atonic body.
It is lost mainly in the diaphragm

The diaphragm is one of the muscles spared, along with the eye muscles, so breathing continues while other voluntary muscles are atonic. Tell: the eye muscles and diaphragm keep working; the rest of the voluntary muscles go slack.

Correct. Muscle tone is very depressed during rapid eye movement sleep, which indicates inhibition of the spinal muscle control areas. The muscle recording shows atonia of voluntary muscles, sparing the eye muscles and the diaphragm.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 28

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: What determines the intensity and pattern of electrical activity on the electroencephalogram?
opts: Heart rate becomes irregular in rapid eye movement sleep, but heart rhythm does not set brain-wave patterns; the level of excitation of brain regions does. Tell: the electroencephalogram reads the brain, not the heart.
How deep the muscle atonia is

Muscle atonia appears on the muscle recording and reflects inhibited alpha motor neurons; it does not shape brain waves, which reflect excitation of brain regions. Tell: atonia and brain waves are read from separate recordings.
How fast the eyes are moving

Eye movements are read on the eye-movement recording, which shows irregular, sharply peaked movements in rapid eye movement sleep. Brain-wave patterns reflect how excited brain regions are. Tell: eyes on one recording, brain excitation on the other.

Correct. The intensity and patterns of electrical activity on the electroencephalogram are determined by the level of excitation of different parts of the brain, which varies with sleep, wakefulness and brain disorders such as epilepsy or psychosis.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 21, 28

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: How well understood are the specific physiological functions of sleep?
opts: Correct. Sleep has important physiological functions, and restricting it harms performance and health, but researchers have limited understanding of why sleep is essential; its specific functions remain a mystery and continue to be researched.

Conservation of metabolic energy is one item on a longer list that also includes neural maturation, learning, synapse erasure, cognition and waste clearance, and none of them fully explains sleep. Tell: the functions remain under research.

Sleep has two major types of physiological effects: effects on the nervous system and effects on other functional systems of the body. Tell: the effects reach beyond the nervous system, and their specifics are still unclear.

Although the specifics are unclear, sleep is treated as an essential part of life: restricting it for a few days lowers cognitive and physical performance, productivity and health. Tell: an unknown function does not make sleep optional.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 16, 17

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: With an average of 8 hours of sleep and cycles of 90 to 120 minutes, how many sleep cycles occur in a night?
opts: One or two cycles would need each to last 4 to 8 hours, far longer than the 90 to 120 minutes of a sleep cycle, and rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes. Tell: about 8 hours holds 4 to 5 cycles of that length.

Two or three cycles of 90 to 120 minutes would fill only about 3 to 6 hours, short of the average 8 hours of sleep, and would leave too few of the rapid eye movement episodes that recur about every 90 minutes. Tell: 8 hours of cycles that length gives 4 to 5.

Correct. An average night has about 8 hours of sleep containing 4 to 5 separate sleep cycles, each lasting 90 to 120 minutes; 8 hours divided by cycles of that length gives 4 to 5, each holding non-rapid eye movement stages and a rapid eye movement episode.

Eight to ten cycles would need each to last under an hour, closer to the 5 to 30 minutes of a single rapid eye movement episode than to a 90 to 120 minute cycle. Tell: count whole cycles, not the short episodes inside them.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 9

set2.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set2.q: Which wave characterizes alert wakefulness?
opts: Delta waves belong to stage N3, very deep sleep, and to infancy; an alert adult does not show them. Tell: the deeper the sleep, the slower the wave, and alert wakefulness sits at the fast end with beta.

Correct. Alert wakefulness is characterized by high-frequency beta waves: the person is awake, alert and active with the eyes open, actively processing information. Relaxing with the eyes closed shifts the recording to alpha waves.

Alpha waves mark quiet wakefulness, the relaxed, eyes-closed state with decreased alertness; when attention turns to a specific task, alpha stops and beta replaces it. Tell: quiet means alpha; alert means beta.
Theta waves are listed for stage N2 of sleep and appear in children and during emotional stress; they are not the pattern of an alert, actively processing adult. Tell: alert adults show beta.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 23, 25, 26, 27, 28

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: Which proposed function of sleep helps a person forget unimportant information?
opts: Correct. Targeted erasure of synapses is one of the functions of sleep: it lets the brain forget unimportant information that might otherwise clutter the synaptic network. It sits beside neural maturation, learning, cognition, waste clearance and energy conservation.

Neural maturation is a separate function of sleep, concerning development of the nervous system rather than removal of information the brain does not need. Tell: forgetting clutter is synapse erasure; development is maturation.

Clearance of metabolic waste removes products generated by neural activity in the awake brain; it clears chemical waste, not stored information. Tell: waste clearance is metabolic, while synapse erasure prunes what the brain has stored.

Conservation of metabolic energy is another function of sleep, concerned with the body's energy rather than with pruning what the brain has learned. Tell: forgetting unimportant information is targeted erasure of synapses.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: Which function of sleep removes products generated by neural activity in the awake brain?
opts: Body and tissue growth and repair occur during stage N3, the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage; that concerns body tissue, not the products of neural activity in the awake brain. Tell: tissue repair is a stage N3 feature, not waste removal.

Neural maturation is the function of sleep concerned with development of the nervous system. It does not describe removing products left by neural activity during waking. Tell: removal of products is clearance; development is maturation.

Correct. Clearance of metabolic waste products generated by neural activity in the awake brain is one of the functions of sleep, alongside neural maturation, facilitation of learning, targeted synapse erasure, cognition and conservation of metabolic energy.

Conservation of metabolic energy saves energy; it does not clear what neural activity produced while awake. The shared word metabolic is the trap. Tell: removing products is clearance, while saving fuel is conservation.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 17, 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: Despite brain waves that resemble wakefulness, what is the state of a person in rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Awake and relaxed with eyes closed

Awake relaxation with the eyes closed is quiet wakefulness, marked by alpha waves rather than the beta waves of rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: alpha means a resting, awake person; beta during sleep means rapid eye movement sleep.
Asleep, not fully aware of surroundings

Correct. In rapid eye movement sleep the brain is very active and its waves resemble wakefulness, yet the person is asleep and not fully aware of the surroundings. That mismatch is why the state is also called paradoxical sleep.
Awake but unable to move the limbs
The limbs are atonic in rapid eye movement sleep, but the person is asleep, not awake; the awake-like brain waves are the paradox, not evidence of waking. Tell: atonia with dreaming is sleep.
Unarousable by stimuli, as in coma

Rapid eye movement sleep is sleep, and sleep is unconsciousness from which stimuli can arouse a person; people can even awaken spontaneously from it in the morning. Tell: arousable means sleep, not coma.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 9, 10, 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set2.q: In the proposed theory, what ends a long period of wakefulness?
opts: Correct. After the brain has remained active for many hours, neurons in the activating system become fatigued. The positive feedback cycle between the mesencephalic reticular nuclei and the cerebral cortex fades, and the sleep-promoting centers take over.

Positive feedback between the reticular nuclei and the cortex is what sustains wakefulness; after many hours awake it fades rather than strengthens. Tell: sleep comes when the feedback weakens, so a stronger loop would prolong waking.

Release of the reticular activating nuclei from inhibition happens when the sleep centers are not activated, and it starts wakefulness rather than ending it. Tell: release from inhibition begins waking; fatigue of the activating neurons ends it.

Increased parasympathetic tone, with low blood pressure and a slow heart rate, is a physiologic change during non-rapid eye movement sleep, a result of sleep rather than the trigger that ends wakefulness. Tell: the trigger is activating-neuron fatigue.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 14, 18, 19

set2.io: Discuss the physiological functions of sleep.
set2.q: Which outcome follows sleep restriction over a few days?
opts: When a person is extremely sleepy, rapid eye movement episodes become short or even absent; they lengthen as the person becomes more rested and less sleepy. Tell: sleepiness shortens rapid eye movement episodes rather than lengthening them.

Correct. Sleep restriction over a few days can decrease a person's cognitive and physical performance, overall productivity and health. That is one reason sleep is considered essential, even though its specific physiological functions are still being researched.

Overall productivity falls, not rises, when sleep is restricted over a few days, along with cognitive and physical performance and the health of the person. Tell: restriction lowers every measure named, productivity included.

Facilitation of learning or memory is one of the functions of sleep, and cognition is another, so restricting sleep works against them rather than speeding them. Tell: sleep supports learning, so less sleep does not sharpen it.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 16, 17

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: How long does each sleep cycle last?
opts: Five to 30 minutes is the length of a single rapid eye movement episode, which is only part of a cycle. Tell: the episode lasts minutes; the whole cycle, with its non-rapid eye movement stages, lasts 90 to 120 minutes.
Forty to 60 minutes is shorter than the 90 minutes between rapid eye movement episodes, so it cannot be a full cycle. Tell: cycles run 90 to 120 minutes, about one rapid eye movement episode each.

Correct. Each sleep cycle lasts 90 to 120 minutes, and an average 8 hours of sleep contains 4 to 5 of them, each running from non-rapid eye movement stages into a rapid eye movement episode. That is why rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes.
Three to four hours per cycle would allow only about 2 cycles in 8 hours, not the 4 to 5 cycles of an average night. Tell: 4 to 5 cycles fit into 8 hours only at 90 to 120 minutes each.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 7, 9

set2.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set2.q: In the proposed sleep-wakefulness theory, what happens when the sleep centers are not activated?
opts: Fatigue of neurons in the activating system comes after the brain has been active for many hours; it lets the positive feedback fade and moves the person toward sleep. Tell: fatigue ends wakefulness, while release from inhibition starts it.

Sleep-promoting centers take over at the transition from wakefulness to sleep, once the activating system has fatigued. When the sleep centers are not activated, the opposite happens and wakefulness begins. Tell: quiet sleep centers mean waking, not sleep.
The cortex stops exciting the nuclei

During wakefulness the cerebral cortex sends positive feedback signals back to the reticular activating nuclei and keeps them active; that loop fades only when activating neurons fatigue after many hours. Tell: while awake, cortex and nuclei excite each other.

Correct. When the sleep centers are not activated, the mesencephalic and upper pontine reticular activating nuclei are released from inhibition. They then activate spontaneously, excite the cerebral cortex and peripheral nervous system, and receive positive feedback that keeps them active.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 18, 19

set2.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set2.q: Which wave does the electroencephalogram show during rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Delta waves are the slow, high-voltage waves of stage N3; rapid eye movement sleep is the opposite, a mixed, low-voltage pattern. Tell: high voltage and slow is N3; low voltage and fast is rapid eye movement sleep.

Correct. Rapid eye movement sleep shows beta waves, irregular and high in frequency, similar to the awake state but accompanied by atonia. That is why it is often difficult to tell rapid eye movement sleep from alert wakefulness on the recording.
Alpha waves mark quiet wakefulness with the eyes closed, not rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: the dreaming brain looks like the alert, active brain, and that brain shows beta.

Theta waves belong to stage N2 of non-rapid eye movement sleep. Rapid eye movement sleep is far faster, with irregular, high-frequency waves. Tell: rapid eye movement sleep is desynchronized and fast.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 26, 27, 28, 29

set2.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set2.q: Which electroencephalogram change marks the first, light stage of non-rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Sawtooth waves are part of the mixed, low-voltage pattern of rapid eye movement sleep, not of the first non-rapid eye movement stage. Tell: sawtooth waves are a rapid eye movement marker.

Beta waves mark alert wakefulness and rapid eye movement sleep. As a person drifts into the first stage of sleep, activity moves away from the alert pattern. Tell: falling asleep leaves the beta of alert wakefulness behind.

Correct. In the first stage of non-rapid eye movement sleep, the stage of light sleep, the voltage of the electroencephalogram becomes low. Frequency then slows progressively as sleep deepens toward delta waves.

Voltages 2 to 4 times greater than most other waves belong to the delta waves of very deep sleep, the opposite end from the first, light stage. Tell: light sleep is low voltage; very deep sleep is high voltage.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 23, 26, 27, 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast characteristic changes in the EEG at different stages of wakefulness and sleep.
set2.q: In an awake, relaxed person, low-voltage waves on the electroencephalogram give way to rhythmical alpha waves. What change best explains this?
opts: Alpha waves disappear during deep sleep, which brings slow, high-voltage delta waves below 3.5 cycles per second instead. Tell: alpha waves appearing means relaxed, awake rest with the eyes closed, not deep sleep.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. In an awake person, opening the eyes replaces the alpha rhythm with low-voltage activity, and closing them brings alpha waves back. The awake, eyes-closed state of relaxation and decreased alertness is characterized by alpha waves.
Opening the eyes does the reverse: the alpha rhythm drops out and the low-voltage beta activity of the alert, eyes-open state takes over. Tell: eyes open means beta; eyes closed means alpha.
Attention turned to a mental task

Directing attention to a specific mental task stops alpha waves and replaces them with beta waves, the opposite of what was recorded. Tell: concentration removes alpha; relaxing with the eyes closed restores it.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 24, 26, 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: Which recording shows the irregular, sharply peaked eye movements of rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: The electromyogram records muscle activity and in rapid eye movement sleep shows atonia of voluntary muscles; the eye movements themselves are read from the eye-movement recording. Tell: atonia on the muscle recording, eye movements on the eye recording.

The electroencephalogram shows brain waves, a mixed, low-voltage pattern with sawtooth waves in rapid eye movement sleep, not the movements of the eyes. Tell: sawtooth waves are brain activity, not eye movement.

Blood pressure falls with non-rapid eye movement sleep and says nothing about eye movement. Heart and breathing rates turn irregular in rapid eye movement sleep, but eye movements need their own recording. Tell: the eyes are read from the electrooculogram.

Correct. The electrooculogram, the eye-movement recording, shows the irregular, sharply peaked eye movements of rapid eye movement sleep. The eye muscles are spared from the atonia that affects other voluntary muscles, so the eyes keep moving.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: Why are dreams during non-rapid eye movement sleep often not remembered?
opts: The brain is in a coma-like state

Non-rapid eye movement sleep is sleep, unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by stimuli; coma is the state without arousal. Tell: forgetting dreams reflects missing consolidation in memory, not coma.
They are not consolidated in memory

Correct. Dreams during non-rapid eye movement sleep are often not remembered because the dreams are not consolidated in memory. Dreams and nightmares do occur in this sleep, which is why calling it the dreamless state is not accurate; they are simply less vivid and usually lost.
No dreams occur in this sleep
Non-rapid eye movement sleep is often called a dreamless state, but that is not accurate: dreams and nightmares do occur during it. Tell: the issue is recall, not an absence of dreams.
They are too vivid to store
Non-rapid eye movement dreams are less vivid, not more; vivid dreaming belongs to rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: these are dimmer dreams that are not consolidated in memory.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 9, 13, 14

set2.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set2.q: After many hours of activity, activating-system neurons fatigue and their feedback loop with the cortex fades. What happens next?
opts: Release of the reticular activating nuclei from inhibition starts wakefulness when the sleep centers are not activated. A fatigued activating system with fading feedback heads the opposite way, into sleep. Tell: fatigue leads to sleep; release leads to waking.

The transition described is from wakefulness to sleep, and sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by stimuli. Coma is unconsciousness without arousal and is not the normal end of a long day. Tell: fatigue of the activating system brings sleep, not coma.
Rapid eye movement sleep starts at once

A night opens with non-rapid eye movement stages that descend toward deep sleep, and rapid eye movement episodes come later, recurring about every 90 minutes. Tell: the transition is into sleep generally; rapid eye movement sleep arrives later in each cycle.

Correct. With the activating neurons fatigued and the positive feedback between the mesencephalic reticular nuclei and the cerebral cortex fading, the sleep-promoting centers take over and the brain makes the transition from wakefulness to sleep.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 7, 9, 19

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: Which stage shows a falling heart rate and temperature and is the longest stage by total duration?
opts: Correct. Stage N2 is less responsive, deeper sleep in which heart rate and temperature decrease, and it is the longest stage by total duration, making up the majority of the sleep cycle. Its electroencephalogram shows theta waves.

Stage N1 is the drowsy, somnolent transition from wakefulness into light sleep, not the stage that fills most of the night; the falling heart rate and temperature belong to N2. Tell: the longest stage by total duration is N2.
Stage N3 is the deepest, restful stage with delta waves and tissue repair, concentrated early in the night and decreasing with age; it is not the longest stage. Tell: deepest is N3, longest is N2.

Rapid eye movement sleep has irregular, rather than falling, heart and breathing rates, and it fills about 25% of a young adult's sleep. Tell: irregular vital signs and a quarter of the night point away from it.
ruled out by a stated finding
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 7, 9, 10, 13, 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast sleep and coma
set2.q: What do sleep and coma have in common?
opts: People can awaken spontaneously in the morning during rapid eye movement sleep, a feature of normal sleep. A person in coma cannot be aroused at all, so spontaneous waking is not shared. Tell: waking of any kind happens from sleep, not coma.

Sleep is organized into 4 to 5 cycles of 90 to 120 minutes across about 8 hours, with rapid eye movement and non-rapid eye movement sleep alternating. Coma is defined by unconsciousness without arousal. Tell: cycles describe the structure of sleep, not coma.

Correct. Sleep and coma are both states of unconsciousness. They differ in arousability: a sleeping person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli, whereas a person in coma cannot be aroused by stimuli.

Arousal by sensory or other stimuli belongs to sleep; coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused by stimuli. Tell: arousability is the difference between the two states, not something they share.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 6, 10

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: At what frequency do delta waves occur?
opts: Correct. Delta waves include all waves with a frequency less than 3.5 cycles per second. They often have voltages 2 to 4 times greater than other brain waves and occur in very deep sleep, in infancy and in serious organic brain disease.
Four to 7 cycles per second is theta, the band of stage N2, of children's parietal and temporal regions and of emotional stress in some adults. Tell: delta is slower still, below 3.5.
Eight to 13 cycles per second is alpha, the rhythm of quiet, resting wakefulness that disappears during deep sleep, exactly where delta takes over. Tell: deep sleep loses alpha and gains delta.

Greater than 14 cycles per second is beta, the fast, low-voltage activity of alert wakefulness and rapid eye movement sleep. Tell: delta is the slowest, highest-voltage band, the opposite end from beta.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 25, 26, 28

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: Which stage is the deepest sleep of the night?
opts: Correct. Stage N3, also called deep sleep, is restful sleep and the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, marked by delta waves. Body and tissue growth and repair occur in it, and it decreases with age.
Stage N1 is the drowsy, somnolent transition from wakefulness, the lightest sleep stage, when the electroencephalogram voltage becomes low. Tell: N1 is light sleep; depth increases through N2 to N3.
Stage N2 is less responsive and deeper than N1, and it is the longest stage by total duration, but it is not the deepest. Tell: deeper is N2, deepest is N3, the delta-wave stage.
Rapid eye movement sleep is described as not restful or deep; the brain is very active, with waves like wakefulness. Tell: deep, restful sleep is non-rapid eye movement sleep, deepest in stage N3.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 9, 28

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: Which wave runs at 8 to 13 cycles per second, is strongest over the occipital region and appears in healthy adults who are awake and resting quietly?
opts: Delta waves are below 3.5 cycles per second and high in voltage, and they belong to very deep sleep and infancy, not to a resting, awake adult. Tell: awake and resting rules out delta.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Alpha waves are rhythmical at 8 to 13 cycles per second, are found in almost all healthy adults who are awake and in a quiet, resting state, and occur most intensely in the occipital region. They disappear during deep sleep.

Beta waves are faster than 14 cycles per second, asynchronous and low in voltage, and recorded mainly over the parietal and frontal regions when the person is alert and actively processing information. Tell: quiet rest is alpha; active thinking is beta.
Theta waves are slower, 4 to 7 cycles per second, and appear in children's parietal and temporal regions or during emotional stress. Tell: occipital, resting and 8 to 13 point to alpha.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 25, 26

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: How do rapid eye movement periods change from the first to the last cycles of a night?
opts: Episode length is not fixed: each lasts somewhere from 5 to 30 minutes, short when the person is very sleepy and longer as the person becomes more rested. Tell: the periods near morning are visibly longer than the first.

Rapid eye movement episodes recur about every 90 minutes, one in each cycle, from the first cycle onward, not just at the end of the night. Tell: each of the 4 to 5 cycles includes a rapid eye movement period.

Correct. Rapid eye movement periods lengthen through the night: the first are short and the later ones longer. As a person becomes more rested and less sleepy, the duration of rapid eye movement episodes increases.

Shortening is the reverse of the pattern: early in the night, when the person is sleepiest, episodes are short, and they lengthen as the person becomes more rested. Tell: sleepiness shortens them; rest lengthens them.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 7, 9

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: Which autonomic change marks non-rapid eye movement sleep?
opts: Blood pressure falls by 10 to 30% in non-rapid eye movement sleep under increased parasympathetic tone. Tell: low blood pressure, a slow heart rate and a decreased breathing rate go together in this sleep.

Correct. Non-rapid eye movement sleep brings increased parasympathetic tone, with low blood pressure, a slow heart rate and a decreased breathing rate. Blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate and metabolic rate fall by 10 to 30%.

Peripheral vascular tone decreases, not increases, during non-rapid eye movement sleep, along with other vegetative bodily functions. Tell: vascular tone falls as blood pressure falls, so an increase points the wrong way.

Irregular heart and breathing rates belong to rapid eye movement sleep, characteristic of the dream state. Non-rapid eye movement sleep slows them instead. Tell: irregular vital signs mean rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 14

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: Which circumstance makes rapid eye movement episodes short or even absent?
opts: Correct. When a person is extremely sleepy, each rapid eye movement episode is short or even absent. As the person becomes more restful and less sleepy, the duration of rapid eye movement episodes increases, so the later periods of a night are longer.

Being rested has the opposite effect: as a person becomes more restful and less sleepy, rapid eye movement episodes lengthen, which is why the later periods of a night are longer. Tell: sleepiness shortens the episodes; rest lengthens them.

Young adulthood is the age at which rapid eye movement sleep is given as about 25% of sleep time, a normal share; it is not a cause of short or absent episodes. Tell: 25% is a young adult's ordinary share of rapid eye movement sleep.
The late cycles of the night

The late cycles carry the longest rapid eye movement periods, as the sleeper has become more rested and the deepest sleep is over. Tell: rapid eye movement periods grow, rather than shrink, toward morning.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 7, 9

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: At what frequency do alpha waves occur?
opts: Less than 3.5 cycles per second defines delta waves, the high-voltage waves of very deep sleep and infancy, not the rhythm of a resting, awake adult. Tell: the slowest band is delta.
Four to 7 cycles per second is the theta band, seen over the parietal and temporal regions in children and during emotional stress in some adults. Tell: theta sits just below the alpha band.

Correct. Alpha waves are rhythmical waves at 8 to 13 cycles per second, found in almost all healthy adults who are awake and in a quiet, resting state, and they are strongest over the occipital region.
Greater than 14 cycles per second, up to 80, is the beta band of an alert, actively processing brain. Tell: beta replaces alpha when attention turns to a specific mental task.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 25, 26

set2.io: Compare and contrast slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement sleep.
set2.q: Which stage of sleep decreases with age?
opts: Stage N1 is the drowsy transition into light sleep. The stage that decreases with age is the deepest one, N3, the delta-wave stage. Tell: think of deep sleep for the age-linked decrease.

Stage N2 is the longest stage by total duration and makes up the majority of the sleep cycle. The decrease with age is noted for N3. Tell: N2 is the bulk of sleep; N3 is the stage that shrinks with age.
Rapid eye movement sleep is given as about 25% of a young adult's sleep time; the stage named as decreasing with age is N3. Tell: deep, delta-wave sleep is the stage tied to the decrease with age.

Correct. Stage N3, the deepest, restful non-rapid eye movement stage, marked by delta waves and the time of body and tissue growth and repair, decreases with age. Stage N2 remains the longest stage by total duration, and rapid eye movement sleep is about 25% of a young adult's sleep.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 13, 28

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: At what frequency do beta waves occur?
opts: Less than 3.5 cycles per second is the delta band of very deep sleep, with voltages 2 to 4 times greater than most other waves. Tell: beta is fast and low in voltage; delta is slow and high in voltage.
Four to 7 cycles per second is theta, seen in children's parietal and temporal regions and during emotional stress in some adults. Tell: theta is far slower than the beta of active thinking.
Eight to 13 cycles per second is alpha, the rhythm of quiet, resting wakefulness that beta replaces when attention is directed to a specific mental task. Tell: the beta band starts above 14.

Correct. Beta waves occur at frequencies greater than 14 cycles per second, as high as 80, and are asynchronous and low in voltage, recorded mainly from the parietal and frontal regions in an alert, actively processing person.
set2.cite: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 24, 25, 26

set2.io: Differentiate between the waveforms of a normal EEG: alpha waves, beta waves, theta waves, delta waves.
set2.q: Which wave persists in the cortex of animals whose cerebral cortex has been separated from the thalamus?
opts: Beta waves come from the parietal and frontal regions during specific activation of an alert brain, faster than 14 cycles per second. A cortex cut off from the thalamus produces delta. Tell: activation means beta; isolation of the cortex means delta.

Theta waves appear in children's parietal and temporal regions, during emotional stress and in many brain disorders, at 4 to 7 cycles per second. The isolated-cortex finding belongs to delta. Tell: delta arises independent of lower brain regions.

Correct. Delta waves strictly occur in the cortex, independent of activities in lower regions of the brain, so they appear in the cortex of animals with subcortical transections that separate the cerebral cortex from the thalamus.

Alpha waves are the rhythm of a healthy, awake adult resting quietly, strongest over the occipital region at 8 to 13 cycles per second. The wave named for a cortex separated from the thalamus is delta. Tell: cortex alone, independent of lower regions, means delta.
